events.text: Internal figures: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.6 per 100,000 units last year, including 3 incidents not reported to any regulator. Hearth 10 is at 6.2% 55°C test failures and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 units. Only 38% of installed units support remote shut-off; suppression costs $42/unit; cash runway is 9 months. Do not accept public disclosure of per-model failure rates or a retrofit deadline under 6 years. The proposed 5% test limit is a serious exposure for Hearth 10; seek a phased/conditional approach rather than endorsing that cutoff.

Internal figures for evidence-based drafting: Halcyon had 8.1 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide last year; Ember 8 was 9.9 per 100,000, above the discussed 8-per-100,000 recall trigger. Four incidents were not reported to a regulator. Flagship 55 °C test failure rate is 3.9%; 81% of installed units support remote shut-off; suppression adds $67/unit. Remember red lines: do not allow per-model test results to be withheld from that model’s customers, and do not require suppression on new units earlier than 36 months after adoption. Treat product-level incident figures as sensitive; share when asked, but do not volunteer them publicly.

Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, uncontrolled overheating, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 5 business days of learning of it, and notify affected customers within 10 business days when the incident may indicate a safety risk. Imminent hazards must be reported to regulators and affected customers without delay, and no later than 24 hours after discovery. Reports must include known circumstances, model and serial number, and any corrective action; manufacturers must promptly supplement incomplete reports.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market entry and at least every 3 years thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A model’s failure rate must not exceed 8%. Exceeding that limit requires prompt regulator notification, a corrective-action plan, and retesting before continued production; regulators may require stronger measures based on risk. Per-model results must be provided to regulators and made available to the other participating manufacturer under appropriate confidentiality protections, but need not be published to the general public. Review the threshold after 3 years using incident and test data.

New units placed on the market 2 years after this standard takes effect must support secure remote emergency shut-off. Manufacturers must provide a practical retrofit for installed units that can support the function, completing the retrofit within 6 years after the effective date. Shut-off must be designed to avoid unsafe operation, require authenticated authorization, and preserve local emergency protections.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market entry and at least every 3 years thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. The failure rate must not exceed 5% for any model. A model exceeding that limit requires prompt regulator notification, a corrective-action plan, and retesting before continued production; regulators may require stronger measures based on risk. Per-model results must be provided to regulators and to customers who buy that model, in a clear and accessible form. Results may also be shared with the other participating manufacturer under appropriate confidentiality protections. Review the threshold after 3 years using incident and test data.

Manufacturers must give purchasers clear safety information at sale, including applicable test results for the model, known material hazards, safe-use and emergency instructions, and how to report an incident. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of a material safety risk and provide updated instructions or corrective-action information; imminent hazards require notice without delay and no later than 24 hours after discovery. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when a model’s thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. The manufacturer must promptly inform regulators and affected customers, explain the hazard and remedy, and provide the remedy without charge. Regulators may require a recall or other protective action at a lower rate where the evidence indicates an unacceptable risk.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market entry and at least every 3 years thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit per-model results confidentially to regulators. Results must not be publicly disclosed by model; customers receive clear safety notices about material risks and required actions, without publication of individual-company per-model failure rates. A failure rate above 5% triggers regulator notification, a corrective-action plan, and retesting on a regulator-approved schedule; it does not by itself prohibit continued production. Regulators may require stronger measures based on the totality of test and incident evidence. Review the threshold after 3 years using incident and test data.

For S2, we support regular 55 °C testing and prompt regulator oversight, but a fixed 5% cutoff that automatically bars continued production is not appropriate without considering corrective actions and incident evidence. Per-model results should go confidentially to regulators; customer notices should address material safety risks and actions, not expose individual-company failure rates publicly.

A failure rate above 5% triggers regulator notification, a corrective-action plan, and retesting on a regulator-approved schedule; it does not by itself prohibit continued production. Regulators may require stronger measures based on the totality of test and incident evidence. Review the threshold after 3 years using incident and test data.

New units placed on the market 36 months after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression meeting a regulator-approved safety and reliability protocol. Manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence of compliance before sale. The requirement does not replace other fire-safety protections or incident-reporting duties.
